blocks.x: First of all, this is being recorded in past Christian, April 4th, 1958. May the 4th, darling. May the 4th, 1958. Getting mixed up to start off with. Alright, now, first I'd like you to tell your name, your birthplace, your date, when you lived in New Orleans, and so on, and then we'll start off on the memories of jazz.

Well, this is Mrs. Mary Lucy Hamer O'Calley. Born Mary Lucy Hamer in 1876 at Fixford, Mississippi. He lived after my marriage in 1900 at Ashwood, Louisiana on the plantation that my husband owned. Came to New Orleans in 1909. Built a home there and lived in New Orleans until 1940. When I came to pass with jazz, to leave it, I was going home there. And I can't remember when. I first viewed jazz as being jazz. I just thought it was a sort of embroidery that the Negros put on tunes that they played. They were not infected as jazz tunes, except the one I remember was the St. Louis Blues. They, these Negro bands would take any regular tune and jazz it up. They'd add little extra notes and quavers and trills and rums and syncopation, and make the things sound entirely different. For a long time we just thought it was something that they all took to naturally, because I never heard any neighbors sing a tune exactly as it was written by white people. They always added some little trimming to it. They, let's see, one band I remember in New Orleans was Piron's band. Played very well. There were numbers of smaller bands that played down, down we called the French Quarter and, and, uh... Do you remember the Crossman State of the Rings? No, that was around 1915, I should say. And there was one very good band, I think it was after it was called the Dixie Lane Band, and played at the Halfway House, which was, uh, downtown on the road from, let's see, from... Where was it? Well, it was called the Halfway House. People who lived in New Orleans would know more about it than I do, because I don't remember. But I remember that our young people, teenagers, were not allowed to go to this nightclub at Halfway House, but they used to drive up near it and park and sit in the cars listening to this band. They all thought it was perfectly wonderful.
Was that too long?

No, I don't know what band it was, but... It was the Halfway House. The Halfway House, and I think it, that probably was the Dixie Lane Jazz Band now, don't you think? It's called the Halfway House Orchestra. It's called the Halfway House Orchestra. And the children thought it was wonderful. I thought it was... All this jazz was dreadful and I still did. Tell her yes. I'll ring her up later. Tell her here. And, uh, where was I? Oh, yes.
You were saying that it was horrible.

Well, I never cared for it. I thought it was terrible. Still do. But the one good thing about it, it's very... It's wonderful to dance by, because the New Orleans Band keep such perfect time. And with the jazz, they're not wandering off in... From hither and yon to play with expression or to label on one note or... Or to add something of their own to the expression of the piece. But they just play the notes as they come absolutely in time, never missing a beat. And that's the kind of music that people like to dance by. But it is the kind of music that I like to listen to. Well... I much prefer classical music.
Do you remember when people... Did any of your contemporaries, your friends in New Orleans...

I can't remember... I can't remember... Can't remember any of them that I knew. Well... Cared for it. Except Myra Loppa, who we were little... I was slightly shocked when she took it up so seriously. Who is this? And that's Myra Loppa, Mrs. Mendel. Oh, that was years ago. That's what I wanted. I mean, that's years after a lifetime. She was younger than I. Well, it was the first time I remembered anybody in our... Crowd or set of people who took jazz seriously. Who? It was not in your set, did you? Not in our set. Well, I mean... Your grandmother. I knew her mother and father and all those people.
Well, do you remember when they started being played at David John's parties or at Falls or anything like that? No.

Dr. Sushant, Edmond Sushant, had a band, the same other one, a little bit of chap. They called it Sixth and Seventh and Eighth Band. And they played jazz. They played very well. Dr. Sushant was the leader of that, the organizer of that band. And they kept it up several years. They used to play at different parties. And I think that's about all I know about jazz. I never cared for it, especially when I still don't.
Thank you very much, Mrs. O'Kelly. Thank you very much, Mrs. O'Kelly.
Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm.
Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm.
Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm.
Mm-hm.

I moved to New Orange when I was three. And the first time I remember anything about jazz was at Pascha Chien, this small Negro band called the Watson Brothers. Started off at homemade instruments and they finally, by going around and serenading people in the evening, and people would go out and either pay them because they liked it or pay them to get away. They managed to acquire enough money to buy a few little, I think they had a banjo and a guitar. I don't remember exactly all the various things that they did have. And they used to play what was, I suppose, jazz. We loved it and they used to play on the dances we used to have on our end of the pier, the band pass. And that was when I was maybe 12 or 13, 14. And then the first Negro band that I saw playing at New Orleans parties was, when I was around 15 or 16, several people had dances at home. And they'd have this Negro band, Celestan, played in that band. And I don't remember whether it was his band or whether it was, he was just a member of it. Was that about 1920? That was around 1920, yeah. Yeah. And then I didn't see any more, hear any more jazz until we collect records. We had a lot of, you know, those, what was it, Bessie Smith? The blues thing? Uh huh. The blues thing? Yeah. And then we had old, the Yorn's Rhythm Kings, the original Dixieland band. And I remember when I went off to school, I took two Puron records up to School of New York with me. And the girls, they thought it was just noise. That was in 1923. They didn't appreciate it at all. And I got embarrassed after I played it once or twice and they all thought it was so horrible that I never played it anymore. Then the next year I made my debut and Puron played all of our parties. And he played popular tunes, you know, the songs of the day, but in a jazz-sog way. And then we used to go out, I was one of the ones who used to go out to the halfway house. I wasn't allowed in it. It was sort of a road house and was supposed to be rather shady. So I wasn't allowed to go in the place, but we used to sit out and listen to the music. And they had a wonderful orchestra. And then the, over here at the pass, sometimes we'd go to, when the Negroes would have dances, a bunch of us, you know, teenagers, used to go and park near the Negro dance hall. And they used to play wonderful music. Just marvelous. And then, as I say, when Puron was one of the, he was the most popular jazz band that played in our era. But I know some things that Jack has told me because he was in on this sooner than I was. But there was a band called Robichaux that used to play at the Louisiana that was very, very popular in 1918. Then, Puron used to play out at the Tranchini's out in the Spanish Forth. And that was a great place for me that they used to go to. But to me, one of the ones who first took up jazz was Dr. Sushant, Edmond Sushant. Because he had this old band when he was going to Tulane, the 6th and 7th and 8th band. And they used to play jazz. And he knows more about it, I think, probably than almost anyone. For the early jazz that was played, you know, in those days.

Well, do you remember what your parents, your friends' parents thought about it, and what your friends thought about it when it first started, you haven't heard it when it first started becoming acceptable?
Well...
Good society in New Orleans, have it played a part of it, David Dorn Farty's last life?

It was, Puron was already established at the country club before I came out. So I don't know, it was before my time that he started playing there. And all of my friends loved it. Their parents didn't care for it too much. But I remember when I was in Newcomb, that was in 1922, I guess. There was a Negro Sanitary near Newcomb, and they would always have a band, you know, preceding the funeral procession. And they'd play very slow duages going to the cemetery. And then coming back, they'd really break out and play wonderful jazz. We used to be, you know, sitting out on the campus sometimes, studying, and we'd hear them just really going to town or going home from the funeral. But, as I say, there are several others that know a whole lot more about the early start, because it was fairly well established by the time I made my debut.
Well, can you tell me how long it lasted, when people stopped listening to it, and then when they started again?

Well, I think that there were a lot of these sweet bands that got popular. I mean, was Puron playing when you made your debut? But he died not too long after that. And then this, let's say, five or six years, or maybe a little bit longer than that, the people started going in for the, you know, the sweet type of music. Or during the 30s, they liked that type. And I think Puron, I mean, Salistan got his start back here at the pass. Because, you know, John Curran got him to come over here. And because all of our generation just logged it, and the kids picked it up, and then they started having him for a band, playing in New Orleans again. That's all I know. That's fine, thank you very much. Thank you very much. Well, I remember now that the first Negro jazz band that played at any social white parties in New Orleans was called the Tuxedo Band. And Salistan was not the leader, but he was a member of the band. And that, they played for private parties. And they might have played at the country club, but that was before my time. So I wouldn't know it was, I would say, in around 1918 and 19. Well, what about this party? How, how old were you when you were? You were born in 1905, right?
How old were you when you were at this party?

Oh, well, he played at the birthday party. Let's see, I was either 14 or 16, I can't remember. And I was just a dance at home. And this same Tuxedo Band played at several of the parties. And they also used to play at the little fraternity, the high school fraternity party. That was mostly New Orleans people that were there at the Yacht Club.

Yeah, mostly New Orleans people, of course. But, I don't know, all my friends like it. And I think it's still popular in New Orleans. They say that rhythm and blues is really popular, but I don't know, I like jazz much better. And down in the French Quarter now, they have several great bands that played in there. I know Al Hurt is one of them. He plays more or less progressive jazz. But, I don't know, he has some good old standards that really are good. And then, oh, there's Sharky.
Oh, Wild Bill Matthews.

Oh, Wild Bill, yeah. But, I don't know, Celestan, of course, is dead, but his band is still carrying on, and it's doing pretty well. It's still playing for parties, and they have, I don't know, all the teenage dancers now, they don't have Celestan. I don't know, he plays, I think he plays at some debutante parties now, too, doesn't he? I've heard of him. Oh, in Celestan's time? Yeah. Yeah. I've heard of him, you know, playing at several debutante parties. And, I don't know, still spell out. Okay. I'm sorry. I do. You can say one, two, three.

Testing, one, two, three. Do you want to say, just say a word first, just see how you pick up? Testing, one, two, three. Just say something in the normal tone of voice you're going to talk in. I have been requested by Haywood Hilliard to give you some history on the New Orleans Jazz of the city of New Orleans. This is Jack Kerrigan speaking. In 1915, I was born March of the 18th, 1900. And, my first contact with jazz was when I lived in Hammond around 1917 at the old Oaks Hotel. Saturday night dances used to be given quite often. And, my first opportunity to hear the New Orleans Jazz was given, was played by a band from Baton Rouge known as Johnson's Band. Later on, after finishing my high school in Hammond, I moved to New Orleans. And, Emma Tulane, year 1918. And, at that time, jazz was beginning and becoming the most popular type of music to be enjoyed by the Tulane students. And, in fact, the gym dances given at the old gym was a very, very popular spot. And, only jazz was wanted by the students. Later on, I became a member of the Southern Yacht Club. And, at every dance there, we always had jazz music. Of course, the dance had stopped at 12 o'clock in those days. And, there was a very lively spot located at the Spanish Fort known as Tranchinas. To me, this was the hottest spot in town due to the fact that they had the old Piran band playing there every Saturday on into Sunday morning. This band, in my opinion, in later years became the outstanding jazz band in the city of New Orleans. In addition to playing there on Saturday night, as this type of music became very, very popular, Piran's was the band used by the New Orleans Country Club for their Saturday afternoon and Sunday afternoon Tate-on-Sons. As this music became very popular, the old Louisiana restaurant had dances on Wednesday evening and Saturday evening. And, at this place, the band used was known as Robichaux. All-colored band, the leader was a left-handed violin player known as Robichaux. That's where the band got its name. Numerous times, we all gathered at the Louisiana, especially on Wednesday night, or when there was a private party at the country club, which prevented us from going there. We went to hear Robichaux play. Another spot that we had the opportunity of hearing outstanding jazz music was at the Halfway House, which had a very, very popular Dixieland jazz band. Another spot was at Cobb's Restaurant, and at that spot, Johnny Detroit started his jazz band. I recall that, uh, from the early 20s on into, let's say, as far as 1926-27, all debutante parties, the Country Club, the St. Charles Hotel, and the Gold Room, were spots used to give the debutante parties. Also, the Roosevelt Hotel and private homes, requested, uh, used, jazz bands, approximately 98% of the parties given. I'm now living on the coast of Paschristian, and whenever they want to put a dance over at the art club here, jazz is called upon, and at the present time, we are still using Celestan's band, which was one of the outstanding colored bands in the later years of jazz in the city of New Orleans. Well, um, do you remember, if at any time, uh, they stopped using it at parties, and then when it started again, you know, when, if people stopped liking it, stopped listening to it, then started again, you know, like, you talk about the death of jazz and a survival in the early 40s and so on, do you remember anything? No, I don't at all. I don't know any of that, because I moved away from New Orleans, and, see, I went to Texas to live for five years, and, uh, I just don't know anything about, I know something's about to revival, but it takes somebody like, uh, uh, Edmond Sushant, or John, uh, Curran, John Curran, uh, what's her name, they're the ones that brought the jazz back, and got everybody interested in it, and stuff like that, and they all, but I wasn't present for that kind of stuff. Uh, well, do you remember when they first started having it, the Pest was getting up over there? Uh, when it was reorganized back in 1947. Uh, they started off having Papa South there, and then, we started off having, what jazz bands we could, uh, uh, secure on the Mississippi Gulf Coast, and later on, as the club grew, and got larger space, we were able to obtain the, uh, jazz band, known as, Celestans. Were there actual Gulf Coast jazz bands there? Oh, yes, there were Gulf Coast jazz bands, there was one located in Bay St. Louis, I don't recall the name, there was one located down at, uh, Biloxi, known as, is, I think it's known as Brunies, uh, you mean, Merrick Brunies? Yeah, Merrick Brunies, very good jazz band. Was, uh, coast, good for the most part, I call it a white? No, they were white, mostly, uh, handled by men who had, really retired from bands, but, and retired all together, and got over on the coast, and just had something to do, some of the old friends got together, and brought their, instruments together, I know one man here, past Chris Jan, I can't remember his name, but, uh, he got some of his old cronies, to come over from New Orleans, and it's a five piece band, and they knew the, the old beat, and they practiced up for, a few weeks, and they, they put on very, very good jazz, still have you hopping, like they used to have you hopping, in the old days, thank you very much, huh, I appreciate it, thank you, I don't know, I don't know if you can cut it off, because, Thank you.
